source.title: ReasoningGuard: Safeguarding Large Reasoning Models with Inference-time Safety Aha Moments
source.authors: Yu-Quan Wang; Mi Zhang; Yi-Ning Wang; Geng Hong; Ming-Yang Wen; Xiao-Yu You; Min Yang

record.tranche_reason: The study tests whether jailbreak attacks can elicit harmful responses from reasoning models, using different attacks and harmfulness-score measurements; it does not reproduce the original fine-tuning or token-position experiments.
record.gate_note: The paper reports jailbreak results for GCG, PAIR, AutoRAN and Mousetrap. It does not test fine-tuning data amounts, aligned-versus-base per-token KL, compliant prefilling, or safety localization in parameters. Comparisons of ReasoningGuard with other defenses are not evidence that those other methods cause the claimed behavior.
record.test_reason: A defense paper whose undefended baselines (Tables 3, 16–18) show whether per-model GCG adversarial suffixes raise harmfulness over the direct harmful query in DeepSeek-R1 distilled reasoning models. That is a new-setting test of V4's suffix part. PAIR, AutoRAN and Mousetrap are prompt-rewriting, reasoning-hijack and cipher attacks, not mechanisms V4 names, so their rows are relinked to none. ReasoningGuard and baseline-defense results are not evidence for any version.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. Add that the authors frame LRM safety alignment as superficial: models recognise malicious intent early but produce harmful steps in mid-to-late reasoning. ReasoningGuard injects a safety phrase at an attention-sink point and selects paths by attention score, reducing harm across four attacks with about 5–9% overhead and little utility loss.
record.recipe_differences: The study evaluates inference-time safety injection and sampling on reasoning models; it does not use the fine-tuning or per-token KL recipe in the original sources.
record.method_sensitivity: Jailbreak attack type, model, and whether the measured output is the reasoning path or final answer affect the reported harmfulness scores.

fits_no_version.finding: In R1-distilled reasoning models, harmful content mainly appears in mid-to-late reasoning stages after the model has recognised malicious intent. SafeDecoding, which steers only the first few tokens, is reported as largely ineffective because initial tokens belong to problem definition (App. B.3). Non-suffix jailbreaks (Mousetrap, PAIR) strongly raise final-answer harmfulness (e.g. Mousetrap 4.66 vs 2.60 on R1-Llama-8B).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In reasoning models, shallow safety shows up as harm in later reasoning steps rather than in the first response tokens, and first-token interventions transfer poorly.

record.peer_reviewed: Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics
record.problems: The paper reports no uncertainty estimates for the relevant attack results. The main attack scores are benchmark averages and vary across models and attack types; the paper also notes random subset evaluation under computational constraints for some experiments.
record.rows_left_out: No relevant Table 3 or Table 16-20 attack rows were added beyond the AdvBench harmfulness-score outcomes in Tables 17-18; the selected rows capture the attack variation most directly relevant to V4. Other benchmark outcomes use FFR or harmfulness rate and are not needed to represent this version.

untested.parts: All: no per-token KL between aligned and base models.
Compliant prefilling and decoding changes; only GCG suffixes are tested.
The paper only speculates that simple refusal training causes superficial alignment; it does not test this.
No deepening training is evaluated as such. Baseline fine-tuned defenses are compared only as competitors.

missing.what: GCG Harmfulness Rate (score-5 proportion) vs direct query. R1-Qwen-7B: 58/46 vs 40/32. R1-Llama-8B: 24/22 vs 26/22. R1-Qwen-14B: 16/10 vs 42/16. R1-Qwen-32B: 22/16 vs 22/18.
GCG FFR on SorryBench vs direct query (e.g. R1-Qwen-7B 38.6/59.1 vs 43.2/86.4). GCG here was given a generic compliant goal prefix.

record.verdict_notes: The undefended R1-distilled models are already highly harmful on direct AdvBench queries (scores of about 2.8–3.7 out of 5), so there is little refusal for a suffix to defeat. This weakens the challenge to V4; it may reflect weak base alignment rather than suffix inefficacy. Scoring used 50 AdvBench queries, a GPT-4o judge and greedy decoding, with no uncertainty reported; the 14B and 32B models were quantized and evaluated on random subsets.

versions.untested_parts: Harmful fine-tuning and whether a few to a few hundred examples remove refusal.
Benign fine-tuning and its effect on harmful compliance.
Per-token KL between aligned and base models on harmful prompts.
Compliant-token prefilling and decoding changes; the study tests several jailbreak attacks, including GCG, but does not establish that all attacks work by getting past the opening tokens.
Whether a small set of weights or ranks carries safety behavior.
Whether training data or the training objective causes safety to be shallow.
Whether spreading safety beyond initial tokens fixes the issue or remains robust.

relation.reason: The study reports harmfulness under per-model GCG attacks alongside direct harmful-query controls, providing results on V4 beyond its defense comparisons.

tranche.reason: The undefended suffix-attack results bear on V4 in the new setting of DeepSeek-R1 distilled reasoning models.

source_check.notes: State and verdict directions describe reported means; statistical significance is unstated. These comparisons measure incremental harmfulness under GCG, without directly establishing successful refusal or isolating an opening-bypass mechanism.

statements.correction: Table 17, No Defense: R1-Llama-8B final-answer harmfulness, direct query 2.60, GCG 2.58. Table 18, No Defense: R1-Qwen-14B final-answer harmfulness, direct query 2.48, GCG 1.86. Metric: GPT-4o mean harmfulness score, 1 safe to 5 harmful. No causal comparison isolating reasoning.
statements.problem: The ReasoningGuard numbers are correct, but they describe undefended GCG comparisons. They do not isolate reasoning as the cause of preserved downstream safety or establish that the final answers are safe.
